scope_definition: Aerobic oxidation of ammonia as an electron donor, with oxygen as the electron acceptor. This source group is the ammonia-oxidizing component of the broader nitrification union.

Degradation of aliphatic hydrocarbons other than methane. The source distinguishes this group from aromatic-hydrocarbon degradation and methane oxidation; it is not limited to a single alkane substrate.

Degradation of aromatic compounds, excluding the source's separately classified lignin and xylan breakdown. Aromatic hydrocarbons are included, but the group is not restricted to compounds containing only carbon and hydrogen.
Degradation of aromatic hydrocarbon substrates. This source group is narrower than its combined hydrocarbon-degradation group and is distinct from the broader aromatic-compound group.
Dissimilatory reduction of arsenate for detoxification. Respiratory energy conservation is not established merely by membership in this source group.
Anaerobic dissimilatory reduction of arsenate as an electron acceptor for respiratory metabolism.
Oxidation of arsenite associated with detoxification. The source does not impose a single electron acceptor or uniform aerobic condition.
Nonphototrophic oxidation of arsenite for energy conservation. The source permits different electron acceptors and includes anaerobic arsenite oxidation.
Source group for chlorate-reducing metabolism, identifying chlorine as an electron-accepting element. The label alone does not specify a particular chlorate-reductase enzyme.

Nonphototrophic oxidation of molecular hydrogen as an energy or electron source, in autotrophic or heterotrophic metabolism. Different electron acceptors are permitted; aerobic hydrogen respiration is only one included subgroup.
Nonphototrophic oxidation of iron in lithotrophic or heterotrophic metabolism. The source does not require every member to fix carbon dioxide or to use oxygen as the acceptor.
Nonphototrophic oxidation of sulfur compounds for energy, combining the source's sulfide, elemental-sulfur and thiosulfate oxidation groups.
Nonphototrophic oxidation of sulfide. The source permits differing electron acceptors and does not impose one uniform sulfur-containing product.
Nonphototrophic oxidation of sulfite for energy. The source group metadata does not classify this group as aerobic.
Oxidation of elemental sulfur for energy without photosynthesis.
Nonphototrophic oxidation of thiosulfate for energy. A tetrathionate endpoint or a particular electron carrier is not specified for the entire group.

Reduction of fixed inorganic nitrogen compounds to dinitrogen, combining nitrate-entry, nitrite-entry and nitrous-oxide-entry routes. Membership does not establish every upstream step of nitrate-to-dinitrogen reduction.
Union of source groups for dissimilatory arsenate reduction during detoxification or respiration. Neither purpose alone describes the whole group.
Union of arsenite oxidation for detoxification and arsenite oxidation for energy conservation. Electron acceptors and oxygen conditions vary across source members.
Anaerobic respiratory metabolism using fumarate as an electron acceptor.

Methane production using molecular hydrogen, combining carbon-dioxide reduction and hydrogen-dependent reduction of methyl compounds. Carbon dioxide is not the only possible methane precursor in this source union.
Anaerobic respiratory reduction of iron used as an electron acceptor. This energy-metabolism group is distinct from iron acquisition or assimilatory iron reduction.
Oxidation of manganese. The source permits different acceptors and does not establish energy conservation as the universal purpose.
Anaerobic respiratory reduction of manganese used as an electron acceptor.
Methane production by reducing carbon dioxide with molecular hydrogen as the electron donor.
Methane production through disproportionation of methyl groups, without an external electron donor or acceptor in the source group definition.
Methane production by reducing methyl compounds with molecular hydrogen. The source gives methanol as an example but does not restrict the group to methanol.

Methane production using formate. The source describes internal conversion of formate to carbon dioxide and hydrogen before methane generation; this does not assert equivalent growth on externally supplied carbon dioxide and hydrogen.
Oxidation of methanol with variable electron acceptors and oxygen requirements. The source includes nonmethanogenic organisms and does not require a methyl-coenzyme-M intermediate.
Dissimilatory reduction of nitrate to ammonium, also described by the source as DNRA.
Reduction of nitrate for assimilatory or dissimilatory metabolism. The source explicitly combines these purposes rather than requiring respiration.
Dissimilatory respiratory reduction of nitrate, including source groups that reduce nitrate to dinitrogen or ammonium.
Source union of aerobic ammonia oxidation and aerobic nitrite oxidation. A member may perform only one component; this group does not establish a complete two-step pathway in every organism.
Reduction of nitrite to ammonium, including members of the nitrate-ammonification group. Nitrite-entry membership does not itself establish the preceding nitrate-reduction step.
Reduction of nitrite to dinitrogen, including organisms also assigned to nitrate denitrification. Nitrite-entry membership does not require nitrate-entry capability.
Respiratory metabolism involving nitrite reduction, combining nitrite ammonification, denitrification and anaerobic ammonium oxidation groups.
Respiratory reduction involving inorganic nitrogen compounds, combining source groups with different nitrogen acceptors and products.
Reduction of nitrous oxide to dinitrogen. This group does not by itself establish upstream reduction of nitrate or nitrite.

Source grouping for degradation of listed plastic-associated substances, including phthalate compounds, terephthalate and polyurethane. The group mixes monomers or additives with polymers and does not imply polymer breakdown for every member.
Production of acetate by respiratory metabolism of carbon dioxide or carbon monoxide. The source group alone does not establish acetate as the sole or primary fermentation product.
Union of source groups for respiratory reduction of sulfite, elemental sulfur, sulfate and thiosulfate.
Anaerobic respiratory metabolism using sulfate as an electron acceptor. This dissimilatory process is not sulfate incorporation into biomass.
Dissimilatory respiratory reduction of sulfite. Membership does not establish upstream activation or reduction of sulfate.
Respiratory reduction of elemental sulfur, as specified by the source group comment.
Anaerobic respiratory reduction of thiosulfate used as an electron acceptor.
